column2: In a labour-only model, A needs 2 hours for X and 4 for Y; B needs 6 for X and 8 for Y. A has absolute advantage in both, but B has comparative advantage in Y because its cost is 4/3 X rather than A's 2 X.
column3: In that model, A's absolute advantage in both goods also gives it comparative advantage in both goods.

column2: For opportunity costs of Y equal to 2 X in A and 4/3 X in B, a trade price of 1.5 X per Y lies strictly between the two costs and permits both to gain in the standard model.
column3: With those opportunity costs, a price of 2.5 X per Y permits both countries to gain from specialisation in the standard model.

column2: Under the standard Heckscher-Ohlin assumptions, relative capital abundance and relative capital intensity jointly explain the predicted direction of trade; absolute factory size alone does not determine the prediction.
column3: Under the standard Heckscher-Ohlin assumptions, the country with the larger absolute capital stock must export the capital-intensive good even if its capital-labour ratio is lower.

column1: Specific and ad valorem tariff incidence
column2: At an unchanged specific tariff Rs 20 per unit, a fall in import price from Rs 100 to Rs 80 raises the tariff's ad valorem equivalent from 20% to 25%.
column3: With that price fall and unchanged specific tariff, the ad valorem equivalent falls from 20% to 16%.

column2: A binding import quota can generate rents accruing to licence holders; allocating licences free of charge does not by itself transfer those rents to the government as tariff revenue.
column3: A binding quota with freely allocated licences transfers the entire scarcity rent to the government through the quota's quantitative restriction.

column2: In the standard small-country model with no externalities, an import tariff creates consumption and production deadweight losses and cannot generate a terms-of-trade gain.
column3: In that model, government tariff revenue is a net national gain that necessarily exceeds the consumption and production losses.

column2: A customs union may cause both trade creation and diversion across products, so observing an increase in intra-union trade alone does not determine the sign of the net welfare effect.
column3: An increase in intra-union trade is sufficient to establish a positive net welfare effect even when non-member imports have been displaced.

column1: Rules of origin in a free trade area
column2: With internal tariff removal but different external tariffs, rules of origin address trade deflection through the member charging the lower external tariff.
column3: With different external tariffs in a free trade area, rules of origin primarily create a common external tariff applying to all members.

column2: A customs union adds a common external tariff to internal free trade; a common market further adds factor mobility, which is distinct from adopting a common currency.
column3: Removing internal tariffs and harmonising external tariffs alone establishes a common market even when labour and capital remain immobile.

column2: Merchandise balance -40, net services +25, net primary income -5 and net secondary income +10 imply current-account balance -10 in the stated common units.
column3: Those balances imply a current-account deficit of 40 because the service and income balances belong only to the financial account.

column2: Balance-of-payments accounts balance under double-entry accounting with the relevant balancing entries, while an economy can still experience reserve pressure or a financing difficulty.
column3: Double-entry balancing means the economy cannot experience a balance-of-payments financing difficulty.

column2: A foreign investor's equity acquisition belongs to the financial account under BPM6, while dividend income paid to that investor belongs to primary income in the current account.
column3: Both the equity acquisition and its subsequent dividend payment belong to the financial account because both involve the same foreign investor.

column2: A car producer acquiring a foreign component supplier is backward vertical FDI; establishing foreign production of the same finished car is horizontal FDI.
column3: Acquiring the component supplier is horizontal FDI because both enterprises serve the automobile sector.

column2: A new foreign plant and purchase of an operating foreign plant can both be FDI, while differing in whether productive facilities are newly created or acquired.
column3: Purchasing the operating plant is portfolio investment because the transaction creates no entirely new productive facility.

column2: Licensing can lower the licensor's foreign capital commitment, but weaker direct control and possible dissemination of know-how must enter the entry-mode comparison.
column3: Licensing gives the licensor the same ownership-based operational control as a wholly owned subsidiary while requiring less capital.

column2: A local joint venture may improve access to local knowledge while exposing partners to shared-control and goal-conflict problems.
column3: Local knowledge advantages remove the need to evaluate shared-control and partner-goal conflicts in a joint venture.

column2: A government spending increase is fiscal expansion even if the central bank simultaneously raises its policy rate; the two policy stances can move in opposite directions.
column3: A central-bank rate increase reclassifies the simultaneous government spending increase as contractionary monetary policy.

column2: A policy-rate reduction may fail to induce much new investment when demand expectations are weak or banks do not pass through the reduction fully.
column3: A policy-rate reduction mechanically establishes an equal percentage increase in business investment even with unchanged weak demand expectations.

column2: When public borrowing raises interest rates and displaces some private investment, the fiscal expansion's net demand effect can be smaller than its direct expenditure effect.
column3: Crowding out means the direct public expenditure is not included in aggregate demand and therefore has no initial demand effect.

column2: A firm's voluntary decision to change its organisation is internal; a new binding environmental rule is external even when managers respond by restructuring.
column3: The new binding environmental rule becomes part of the internal environment once management adjusts the organisation to comply.

column2: A project appraisal that explicitly incorporates community harms and mitigation costs applies a stakeholder perspective without logically requiring abandonment of financial viability.
column3: Recognising community harms in project appraisal makes financial viability irrelevant under a stakeholder perspective.

column2: Disclosure must convey material information accurately; repeating a true but immaterial claim does not compensate for concealing a material product risk.
column3: Repeating a technically true advertising claim satisfies the consumer's information interest even when a material product risk is concealed.

column2: Payment for a qualifying imported service and acquisition of foreign equity require different current-account and capital-account analysis under FEMA; BOP labels do not replace the applicable legal test.
column3: Every outward foreign-exchange payment for services must be treated as a capital-account transaction under FEMA because it reduces domestic cash.

column2: A foreign bank establishing a commercial branch illustrates commercial presence, whereas a customer travelling abroad to receive a service illustrates consumption abroad.
column3: The foreign bank's branch and the travelling customer's purchase both illustrate cross-border supply without movement of the supplier or consumer.

column2: An investment-linked local-content requirement raises TRIMS issues; patent-protection obligations fall within TRIPS rather than the services-supply modes of GATS.
column3: An investment-linked local-content requirement is primarily a TRIPS intellectual-property measure because it concerns local production technology.

column2: A bound tariff is a commitment ceiling subject to the applicable rules; an applied tariff can be below that ceiling without changing the bound rate.
column3: An applied tariff below its bound ceiling automatically reduces the bound commitment to the newly applied rate.

column2: MFN concerns treatment across foreign trading partners, while national treatment compares imported products with domestic like products after entry under the relevant rules.
column3: National treatment is the rule requiring identical tariff treatment across every foreign trading partner at the border.

column2: WTO agricultural disciplines distinguish market access, domestic support and export competition; categorising support requires examining the measure rather than only its budget size.
column3: A domestic agricultural subsidy is classified as a market-access tariff solely because its budget affects import demand.

column2: Establishing a qualifying anti-dumping measure requires the relevant dumping, injury and causal analysis; a comparison only with the domestic competitor's price is insufficient.
column3: An import price below a domestic competitor's price by itself establishes dumping, material injury and causation for an anti-dumping measure.

column2: IMF balance-of-payments support, World Bank development finance, UNCTAD trade-and-development work and WTO trade-rule administration serve different institutional functions.
column3: A country seeking adjudication of WTO trade commitments should treat IMF lending conditionality as the WTO dispute-settlement procedure.
